cues.text: A set is a well defined collection of distinct objects.
We may list its members or describe them by a rule.
The set of positive even integers less than eight is two, four, six.
Reordering that list or repeating four does not change the set.
Membership asks whether one object is a member; a subset statement asks
whether
every member of one set belongs to another.
The empty set has no members and is a subset of every set.
A set containing the empty set has one member, so it is different from the
empty set itself.
The power set collects all subsets.
If A has three distinct elements, decide independently whether to include each
element.
Two choices at each of three positions give eight subsets.
The empty set and A itself are included.
A proper subset must differ from A, so seven of those eight are proper.
Do not subtract the empty set merely because it looks unusual.
For the empty set, its power set has one member, namely the empty set.
In set builder notation, always specify the underlying number system and
restrictions.
The equation x squared equals one selects two real numbers, while the
condition
x is a positive real number selects only the positive solution.
Fix the universal set before taking a complement.
Let U contain the integers one through six, A contain one, two, three, and B
contain three, four.
The union contains one, two, three, four; the intersection contains only
three.
The complement of A contains four, five, six.
The difference A minus B contains one, two, whereas B minus A contains four.
Set difference is therefore not commutative.
De Morgan's laws explain how a complement crosses a union or intersection.
Not belonging to either A or B means belonging to both complements, so the
complement of their union is the intersection of their complements.
Not belonging to their intersection means failing at least one membership
condition, so it gives the union of complements.
Intersection distributes over union, and union distributes over intersection.
You can check a proposed identity by following one arbitrary element and its
membership conditions.
For example, membership in A intersect B union C means membership in A and
membership in at least one of B or C.
This becomes the union of A intersect B and A intersect C.
Keep brackets clear: changing them can change the set being described.
Counting union members requires correcting repeated counts.
Suppose a group has forty students, twenty four in A, nineteen in B, and eight
in both.
Adding twenty four and nineteen counts those eight students twice.
Subtract them once to obtain thirty five in at least one set, leaving five in
neither.
Exactly one set contains twenty four plus nineteen minus twice eight, giving
twenty seven.
With three sets, add the three sizes, subtract all three pairwise intersection
sizes, then add the triple intersection once.
Why add it back?
A student in all three was counted three times initially and subtracted three
times, so needs one final count.
For sizes twenty, eighteen, fifteen, pairwise intersection sizes eight, seven,
six, and triple size three, the union has thirty five members.
The number in exactly two sets is the sum of the pairwise sizes minus three
times the triple size, giving twelve.
Pairwise intersection counts ordinarily include students in the third set
unless the wording explicitly says otherwise.
Draw disjoint regions starting at the triple intersection when the data feel
confusing.
Finally, verify that every derived region is nonnegative and that the union
does not exceed the supplied group size.
A binary relation from A to B is a subset of the Cartesian product A cross B.
Each member is an ordered pair, so reversing its entries need not preserve
membership.
For a relation on A, reflexivity requires every pair a, a.
Symmetry says that whenever a, b belongs, b, a also belongs.
Antisymmetry says that if both a, b and b, a belong, then a must equal b.
This is not simply the opposite of symmetry: the identity relation is both
symmetric and antisymmetric.
Transitivity requires a, c whenever a, b and b, c belong.
Consider the less than or equal relation on real numbers.
It is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, but not symmetric.
The relation of having the same absolute value is reflexive, symmetric and
transitive.
To disprove a property, one counterexample is enough.
To establish it for an infinite set, use an argument covering arbitrary
elements rather than checking only a few examples.
The empty relation on a nonempty set is not reflexive, while symmetry and
transitivity hold because no pairs trigger a failure.
Always state the underlying set: changing it can change the truth of a
property.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
These three conditions make its equivalence classes divide the underlying set
into disjoint groups.
On the integers, define a related to b when a minus b is divisible by three.
Reflexivity follows because a minus a is zero, a multiple of three.
If a minus b is divisible by three, its negative b minus a is too,
establishing
symmetry.
If a minus b and b minus c are divisible by three, their sum a minus c is
divisible by three, establishing transitivity.
Integers fall into three classes according to remainder zero, one or two after
division by three.
Negative integers belong too: negative one is in the same class as two because
their difference is negative three.
Every integer belongs to exactly one class, and two classes sharing a member
must be the same class.
This is the partition property.
Conversely, a partition defines an equivalence relation by declaring two
elements related when they lie in the same block.
Do not use a merely symmetric relation as an equivalence relation without
checking transitivity and reflexivity.
For example, being unequal is symmetric on the integers but fails reflexivity
and also fails transitivity.
A function from A to B assigns exactly one element of B to every element of A.
Multiple inputs may share an output, but one input cannot have two different
outputs.
The domain is A, the codomain is B, and the range is the collection of outputs
actually reached.
For the square function from the reals to the reals, negative outputs are
never
reached, so the range is the nonnegative reals and is smaller than the
codomain.
If an algebraic formula is supplied without a domain, first identify the real
inputs where the formula is defined.
For the square root of x minus one divided by x minus three, the square root
requires x at least one, and the denominator excludes three.
Combine the conditions rather than treating either as sufficient.
The domain is from one inclusive to three exclusive, together with numbers
greater than three.
Cancelling a factor does not automatically restore an excluded input from the
original expression.
For example, x squared minus one divided by x minus one agrees with x plus one
only when x is not one.
Writing the original domain prevents an algebraic simplification from silently
defining a different function.
A function is injective, or one to one, when equal outputs imply equal inputs.
It is onto, or surjective, when every member of its codomain is reached.
A function whose range is a proper subset of its codomain is often called
into.
These conditions answer different questions.
The square function from the reals to the reals is neither injective nor onto:
one and negative one share an output, and negative numbers are missed.
Keep the real domain but change the codomain to the nonnegative reals.
It becomes onto but remains noninjective.
Restrict both domain and codomain to the nonnegative reals.
It is now injective and onto, hence bijective.
An affine function two x plus three from the reals to the reals is bijective:
equal outputs give equal inputs, and any target y has input y minus three
divided by two.
A constant function on a domain with at least two elements is not injective,
but it is onto a codomain containing only its constant value.
State the sets every time; a formula alone does not settle the classification.
Use a counterexample to refute injectivity and solve for a preimage to
establish surjectivity.
For a finite domain containing m elements and a finite codomain containing n
elements, each input can independently choose any of n outputs.
This gives n to the power m functions.
With a three element domain and a two element codomain, there are eight
functions.
Exactly two are constant, and the other six hit both target elements, so there
are six onto functions in this particular case.
There are no injections because three distinct inputs cannot have distinct
outputs in only two target positions.
Reverse the sizes: a two element domain and three element codomain give nine
functions and six injections, but no surjections.
An injection uses three choices for the first output and two for the second.
In general, for m no greater than n, the injection count is n factorial
divided
by n minus m factorial.
If m exceeds n, it is zero.
A bijection between two finite sets of the same size n is a permutation of the
targets, giving n factorial choices.
For equal finite sizes, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent, but this
shortcut is not a general rule for infinite sets.
Keep the finite hypothesis attached to the counting argument.
Composition feeds one function's output into another.
In f composed with g, the inner function g acts first.
Let f of x equal two x plus one and g of x equal x squared.
Then f of g of x is two x squared plus one, whereas g of f of x is the square
of two x plus one.
These functions differ, so order matters.
A composite requires x in the domain of g and g of x in the domain of f.
Consider f of u equal one divided by u minus one, and g of x equal the square
root of x.
The composite is one divided by the square root of x minus one.
The inner function requires x at least zero, while the outer denominator
excludes square root of x equal to one, so exclude x equal to one.
Its domain is the nonnegative reals with one removed.
Composition is associative when all the stated maps are compatible, even
though
it is not commutative.
Thus f composed with g composed with h can be bracketed in either association
without reversing their order.
Before cancelling an expression or rearranging a composition, write the
original input conditions so no forbidden point is accidentally restored.
An inverse function undoes a bijection.
If f maps A bijectively onto B, its inverse maps B back to A.
Composing the inverse after f gives the identity on A, and composing f after
its inverse gives the identity on B.
The notation f inverse is not a reciprocal.
For f of x equal two x plus three on the reals, solve y equals two x plus
three
for x.
This gives x equal to y minus three divided by two, so the inverse takes an
input y to that value.
Verify both compositions, not just a symbolic swap.
The square function on all reals has no inverse function because positive and
negative inputs can share an output.
Restrict the original domain to the nonnegative reals and take the nonnegative
reals as codomain.
Then its inverse is the nonnegative square root.
The alternative negative half line produces a different inverse branch.
For f of x equal x squared minus four on x at least zero, the codomain must be
the interval starting at negative four for a bijection.
Its inverse is square root of y plus four.
Domain and codomain restrictions therefore determine which inverse is valid.
